title: Stamp seal (conoid) with animal and divine symbols

altText: A small cone-shaped stone seal with bands of color in the stone, shown with its flat carved face, which has a bull and symbols.

context: A cone-shaped stamp seal of banded chalcedony, made in Mesopotamia between the second half of the 8th and the 6th century BCE. It is about 2.8 centimeters high, and its flat face, about 2.4 by 2.3 centimeters, is carved with an animal, tagged as a bull, and divine symbols.

descriptions.k: This tiny stone looks like a cone. Its flat bottom has a bull carved on it, with some little symbols. The stone has stripes of color. If you pressed it into soft clay, what would you see?
descriptions.g12: This small stone stamp is shaped like a cone. It was made in Mesopotamia more than 2,500 years ago. A bull and special symbols are carved on its flat bottom. The stone has bands of color in it. Press it in clay and the bull would print. Why might someone choose a bull?
descriptions.g35: This conoid stamp seal, shaped like a cone, was carved in Mesopotamia between the late 8th and 6th centuries BCE. It is about 2.8 centimeters tall. The flat face shows a bull and divine symbols, signs that stand for gods. The stone is banded chalcedony, a kind of quartz with stripes of color. When pressed into clay, the carving prints as a picture. What might a bull and symbols tell people about the owner?
descriptions.g68: A conoid stamp seal like this one was a personal mark used on clay in Mesopotamia between the late 8th and 6th centuries BCE. Its flat face, about 2.4 by 2.3 centimeters, shows a bull with divine symbols, which may refer to gods or their powers. The stone is banded chalcedony, whose natural stripes make each seal unique. The design is cut in reverse so it prints correctly. How do the carver's choices make a single bull and a few symbols into a strong, readable image?
descriptions.g910: This conoid seal belongs to a period when Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian traditions overlapped, which is why the museum labels it Assyro-Babylonian. Carved in banded chalcedony, it joins a natural pattern in the stone with a cut design: a bull and divine symbols on a flat face about 2.4 centimeters wide. The reverse carving prints a positive image in clay. Some symbols can be matched to gods through texts and other seals, while others stay uncertain. How do material, scale, and iconography combine to make a personal emblem?
descriptions.g1112: Made between the late 8th and 6th centuries BCE, this conoid seal sits within a time when Assyrian and Babylonian visual cultures overlapped, reflected in its combined cultural label. The bull and divine symbols on its face may have served as emblem, protection, or devotion, though no inscription here fixes their meaning. The banded stone adds a natural pattern that the carver may or may not have exploited. As a stamp seal, it makes one image per pressing, unlike a rolling cylinder. How do we interpret an image when comparison with other seals is our main evidence?

teacherNote.context: A conoid stamp seal in banded chalcedony from Mesopotamia, second half of the 8th to the 6th century BCE, with a bull and divine symbols on its face. The label Assyro-Babylonian reflects overlapping traditions, and the symbols' exact meanings are interpreted by comparison.
directions: Have students design a mark with one animal and two symbols, then print it with a stamp pad or clay to see the reversed image.
Compare this seal with the deer stamp seal and the cylinder seals in the archive.
Discuss how people choose symbols for identity and what those symbols can and cannot say.
